name: Thymosin Alpha 1

b.x: Thymosin Alpha 1 (Tα1, CAS 62304-98-7, molecular weight 3108 Da) is a 28-amino-acid acetylated peptide naturally produced by the thymus gland, approved in 35 countries under the brand name Zadaxin. The US restricted it from compounding pharmacies, creating a regulatory contradiction that defines its story. It binds Toll-like receptors TLR2 and TLR9 on dendritic cells, triggering downstream T-cell differentiation and NK cell activation through MyD88-dependent signaling. The clinical dose is 1.6 mg (1600 mcg) subcutaneously twice weekly, established by decades of Zadaxin prescribing data. The hepatitis B trials built the evidence base. A Phase III RCT (PMC4688733) showed HBeAg seroconversion at 30 to 40% versus 18% on placebo at 12 months. The Dinetz and Lee 2024 review [1] pulled together 30+ trials enrolling 11,000+ subjects and found consistent immune activation across indications. A separate 2024 meta-analysis [2] of 39 RCTs in acute COPD exacerbations (3,329 patients) confirmed improved FEV1, oxygenation, and reduced hospital stay. Community use has expanded well past hepatitis. Longevity practitioners, long COVID patients, and ME/CFS communities use the same 1600 mcg twice-weekly protocol for T-cell restoration. The practical limitation: Tα1 produces no subjective "feel." Bloodwork (CBC with differential, CD4/CD8 ratio) is the only way to confirm it's working. The TESTS Phase 3 sepsis trial (n=1,106) [3] missed its primary mortality endpoint (HR 0.99, p=0.93). That null result is worth knowing. It didn't undermine the hepatitis or immune-support evidence, but it set a boundary on what Tα1 can do in acute critical care.

Tα1 binds TLR2 and TLR9 on dendritic cells. That initial contact triggers MyD88-dependent signaling cascades that upregulate MHC class I and class II expression, improving how dendritic cells present antigens to T cells. Downstream effects split across two immune arms. On the adaptive side, Tα1 drives maturation of CD4+ helper T cells and CD8+ cytotoxic T cells from immature thymic precursors. Even in aged or immunocompromised individuals, it partially restores thymic output of mature T-cell subsets from CD4-/CD8- progenitors. NK cell cytotoxicity increases in parallel. The p38 MAPK and NF-κB pathways carry the cytokine signal. Tα1 pushes Th1-type cytokine production (IL-2, IL-12, IFN-γ) while dampening excessive Th2 responses. This is the immune-balancing property that separates Tα1 from pure immune stimulants. It upregulates regulatory T cells and modulates IDO (indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase) expression, which helps prevent autoimmune overshoot. At the cellular level, Tα1 boosts oxidative killing in macrophages and neutrophils by stimulating NADPH oxidase activity. Pathogens get cleared faster. A single injection triggers signaling cascades on dendritic cells that activate T-cell differentiation responses lasting days to weeks, which explains why twice-weekly dosing works despite the 2-hour plasma half-life.
Thymosin Alpha 1 benefits center on immune modulation and T-cell restoration, with clinical evidence strongest in hepatitis B treatment.
HBeAg seroconversion reached 30 to 40% versus 18% on placebo in hepatitis B patients treated for 6 to 12 months (PMC4688733, Phase III RCT).
T-cell and NK cell activation without stimulant-like effects. Users report no subjective "high" or energy spike; confirmation requires bloodwork showing improved CD4/CD8 ratios and lymphocyte counts.
AECOPD patients showed improved FEV1, better oxygenation, and shorter hospital stays across 39 RCTs enrolling 3,329 patients (meta-analysis 2024) [2].

Post-viral recovery signal in ME/CFS communities. Responders report energy improvement within 24 to 48 hours. Ex vivo data (PMC10030336, n=10 PASC patients) confirmed decreased IL-6, decreased IFN-γ, and increased IL-10.
Vaccine response improvement in elderly and immunocompromised populations, with community and clinical reports of stronger antibody titers when co-administered.
Immune balancing as well as boosting. Tα1 upregulates regulatory T cells and modulates IDO expression, reducing autoimmune overshoot risk compared to pure immune stimulants.

TESTS Phase 3 sepsis trial (n=1,106) [3] failed primary 28-day mortality endpoint. COVID-19 benefit limited to severe/elderly subgroups in meta-analyses; highly heterogeneous (I²=90%). Long COVID evidence is ex vivo only (PMC10030336, n=10).

Limitations

TESTS Phase 3 sepsis trial (PMID 39814420) null result: HR 0.99, p=0.93. COVID-19 meta-analyses: I²=90% heterogeneity: conflicting results driven by study design differences. Long COVID dosing extrapolated from hepatitis B trials. No human longevity RCT. PMID 38308608 is a narrative review from a pro-compounding advocacy position, not a formal systematic meta-analysis.

Community dose (1600 mcg 2x/week) matches clinical standard well. However, community cycling (8–12 weeks on / 4 weeks off) has no clinical trial basis: all trials ran continuous protocols for 6–52 weeks without break periods. Community primary use cases (longevity, long COVID) lack RCT evidence and rely on mechanistic extrapolation from hepatitis B and immunology data.

Reconstitution math for a 10 mg vial with 2.0 mL bacteriostatic water: concentration is 5000 mcg/mL. Total volume is 200 units on a 100-unit insulin syringe (you'll need to refill). Each unit delivers 50 mcg. So 1600 mcg is 32 units, 750 mcg is 15 units. For a 5 mg vial with 2.0 mL bacteriostatic water: concentration is 2500 mcg/mL. Each unit delivers 25 mcg. So 1600 mcg is 64 units, 750 mcg is 30 units. The 10 mg vial is your better value. At 1600 mcg, it holds 6 full injections (10,000 / 1600 = 6.25), just over 3 weeks at twice weekly. A 5 mg vial holds 3. Zinc matters. Tα1 requires zinc as a cofactor for T-cell and NK cell activation. Test RBC zinc before your protocol and supplement 15 to 30 mg zinc glycinate daily if deficient. Skipping this step is probably the most common beginner mistake. Don't judge efficacy by how you feel. Tα1 produces no acute subjective signal. Get bloodwork (CBC with differential, CD4+/CD8+ counts) at baseline and week 8. That's the confirmation window.
Cycling Protocol

In hepatitis B clinical trials, Tα1 was administered at 1.6 mg subcutaneously twice weekly for 6-12 months. For general immune support, shorter courses of 8-12 weeks with a 4-week break are commonly used. Some protocols use continuous low-frequency dosing (1-2x/week) without cycling for chronic immune deficiency. No desensitization or tachyphylaxis has been documented in clinical use.
Thymosin Alpha 1 Cycle

No receptor desensitization, tachyphylaxis, or antibody formation has been documented with TA1 in clinical trials, which ran continuous protocols for 6–52 weeks without break periods. Community cycling (8–12 weeks on / 4 weeks off) is cost-management-driven and community-derived, not pharmacologically required. Some ME-CFS patients report symptom return within 2–3 days of stopping, suggesting continuous dosing may be more appropriate for post-viral indications than cycling.
Symptom return within 2–3 days of stopping (ME-CFS/long COVID users): suggests continuous dosing preferred over cycling for this population
No loss-of-efficacy signal documented in multi-year continuous hepatitis B clinical trials
No hormonal axis suppression, receptor downregulation, or tachyphylaxis mechanism identified

Reconstitute the lyophilized powder Add 2.0 mL bacteriostatic water to a 10 mg vial (yields 5000 mcg/mL) or a 5 mg vial (yields 2500 mcg/mL). Swirl gently. Do not shake. Allow bubbles to settle before drawing.

Draw your dose For 1600 mcg from a 10 mg vial: draw 32 units on a 100-unit insulin syringe. From a 5 mg vial: draw 64 units. All three tiers use this 1600 mcg dose, the Zadaxin label dose (1.6 mg twice weekly).
Choose an injection site Subcutaneous injection in the abdomen (2 inches from navel), thigh, or upper arm. Use a 29 to 31 gauge insulin syringe, 0.5-inch needle. Rotate sites between injections.
Inject subcutaneously Pinch a fold of skin, insert the needle at a 45-degree angle, push the plunger slowly, and hold for 5 seconds before withdrawing.
Timing and frequency Inject twice weekly, spaced 3 to 4 days apart (Monday and Thursday is standard). Morning is preferred. No food or fasting requirements.
Storage after reconstitution Refrigerate at 2 to 8 degrees Celsius. Use reconstituted research-grade peptide within 7 days; pharmaceutical-grade (Zadaxin) is stable longer.

Avoid
Calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus)

Direct pharmacological antagonism: TA1 activates T-cell signaling pathways that calcineurin inhibitors suppress. In transplant recipients, TA1 immune activation risks acute graft rejection. Absolute contraindication in that population.
Systemic corticosteroids (prednisone, dexamethasone, methylprednisolone)

Broad suppression of the immune pathways TA1 activates: co-administration negates TA1 efficacy. Concurrent systemic steroid use also typically indicates an underlying condition (autoimmune flare) where TA1 is itself contraindicated.

Theoretical immune amplification risk outside oncologist-supervised settings. Note: emerging 2024–2025 oncology data (PMID 36871535, ASCO JCO 2024 e16226) suggests the two may add to each other's effect in cancer + reduced ICI-induced colitis: interaction is nuanced and context-dependent. Not for self-research concurrent use.

Organ transplant recipients on immunosuppressive therapy face the most serious risk. Tα1 activates the T-cell signaling pathways that calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus) suppress. In that population, immune activation can trigger acute graft rejection. This is an absolute contraindication. Autoimmune flare acceleration is documented in community and clinic reports. Hashimoto's patients have reported thyroid antibody titer spikes after starting Tα1. MS patients have reported flare acceleration. Lupus patients carrying antinuclear antibodies should check inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR, ANA) before starting and should not use Tα1 during active flare. The confusing part: autoimmune patients actually have lower serum thymosin alpha-1 levels [4]. That makes supplementation seem logical, but Tα1's immune-priming action feeds the same T-cell pathways driving the flare. Published trial safety data across 11,000+ subjects shows a mild profile in non-autoimmune populations. Injection site redness and soreness occur in 5 to 18% of patients across trials. Transient fatigue occurs in 3 to 8%. Flu-like symptoms are rare and resolve within 24 to 48 hours. Myalgia reached 5% in one oncology loading-dose study. ME/CFS and post-viral patients should know about the first-dose immune reaction. A subset experiences 24 to 48 hours of symptom exacerbation after the initial injection. This is an immune activation event, not an allergic reaction. Starting at 750 to 1000 mcg for the first two injections before escalating to 1600 mcg reduces this risk. Interferon-alpha combinations (common in hepatitis protocols) can amplify flu-like side effects through additive immune stimulation. Stacking with other immune-stimulating peptides (LL-37, KPV) carries the same additive activation risk; space injections and start at low doses. Contraindications: pregnancy or breastfeeding (insufficient safety data), known hypersensitivity to Tα1 or formulation components, organ transplant recipients on immunosuppression, active autoimmune diseases in flare, and children under 18. When to seek medical attention: any autoimmune flare symptoms (joint pain, antibody titer rise, sustained fatigue spike), signs of graft rejection in transplant patients, high-grade fever, or allergic reaction (rash, difficulty breathing).
Common Issues & Solutions

No subjective signal: TA1 produces no acute "feel." Confirm benefit via bloodwork (CBC with differential, CD4+/CD8+ counts) at weeks 4 and 8. Most users require lab confirmation to verify efficacy: do not judge by subjective experience alone.

Autoimmune symptom worsening: Hashimoto's antibody titer spikes and MS/lupus flare acceleration documented in community and clinic reports. Pause immediately and check inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR, antinuclear antibodies). Do not restart until flare resolves and immunologist consulted.

Suspected blunted response: TA1 requires zinc as a cofactor for T-cell and NK cell activation. Test RBC zinc before protocol; supplement 15–30 mg zinc glycinate daily if deficient. Also confirm peptide purity (≥98% HPLC): research-grade impurities may reduce bioactivity.

ME-CFS / post-viral first-dose immune reaction: Subset of post-viral patients experience 24–48h symptom exacerbation after first injection: a known immune activation event, not allergy. Mitigate by starting at 750–1000 mcg for first 2 injections, then escalating to 1600 mcg.

Stopping too early with no benefit: Immune priming requires minimum 4–8 weeks. One to two injections will not produce measurable immune changes. Commit to the full 8-week cycle with end-of-cycle bloodwork before evaluating efficacy.

Thymosin Alpha 1 is marketed as Zadaxin (SciClone Pharmaceuticals) and is approved as a prescription drug in over 35 countries for hepatitis B treatment and as an immune adjuvant. It is not FDA-approved in the United States. The FDA designated TA1 as Category II under 503A/503B compounding rules in September 2023, restricting US compounding pharmacy access. That designation was removed in September 2024, but the final 503A determination remains pending. The PCAC committee in December 2024 recommended against 503A approval. FDA's Category 2 page (current as of April 22, 2026) lists Thymosin-alpha 1 (Ta1) among substances withdrawn by their nominators. FDA's May 14, 2026 503A list places it in no category. FDA's March 21, 2025 503B list has thymosin alpha-1 in Category 3, nominated without adequate support. No FDA rule on a 503A listing has followed. TA1 is currently available in the US as a research chemical. It is not scheduled as a controlled substance. Athletes should note that immunomodulatory peptides may fall under WADA prohibited substance categories depending on interpretation; check current WADA guidelines before use in tested competition. This content is for informational purposes only. Thymosin Alpha 1 is not approved by the FDA for any indication in the United States. Nothing on this page constitutes medical advice. Consult a licensed healthcare provider before starting any peptide protocol.

faqs.q: Why only inject 2x/week if the half-life is just 2 hours?
faqs.a: TA1 isn't a hormone that needs sustained blood levels: it's an immune primer. A single injection triggers TLR2/TLR9 signaling cascades on dendritic cells that activate T-cell differentiation responses lasting days to weeks. The 2x/week frequency matches the clinical trials that showed significant immune benefits over 6-12 months. Daily injections wouldn't improve results and just add cost.

faqs.q: Is TA1 safe with autoimmune conditions?
faqs.a: It's context-dependent and potentially risky during active flares. Community reports document Hashimoto's patients seeing antibody titer spikes and MS patients experiencing flare acceleration after starting TA1. The confusing part: autoimmune patients actually have lower serum thymosin alpha-1 levels (PMID 27350088), which sounds like they'd benefit from supplementation. But TA1's immune-priming action stimulates the same T-cell pathways driving the flares. Don't use during active flare; get baseline inflammatory markers first; consult an immunologist.

faqs.q: Why did the FDA restrict TA1 compounding in 2023?
faqs.a: The FDA's 2023 Category II designation under 503A/503B restricted TA1 from compounding pharmacies. A 2024 review (PMID 38308608) covering 30+ trials and 11,000+ subjects directly challenged the decision as inconsistent with the evidence. The restriction wasn't based on adverse event reports. Many US physicians view it as a regulatory gap. The peptide remains available as a research chemical and through international sources.

faqs.q: Can I stack TA1 with checkpoint inhibitors like Keytruda?
faqs.a: Emerging data (PMID 36871535) suggests TA1 may actually synergize with checkpoint inhibitors for antitumor effect while reducing ICI-induced colitis. Clinical studies are underway for NSCLC and melanoma. But combining immune-stimulating agents with checkpoint inhibitors outside oncologist oversight is high-risk. The interaction is nuanced and potentially beneficial in cancer settings, not something to self-manage.

faqs.q: What bloodwork confirms TA1 is working?
faqs.a: Standard monitoring: CD4+ T-cell count, CD8+ count, CD4/CD8 ratio, NK cell activity, CBC with differential. For hepatitis patients, HBV viral load and ALT/AST normalization are the clinical endpoints. For post-viral or long-COVID contexts, T-cell subset analysis showing reversal of exhaustion markers (PD-1, TIM-3) is gold standard but requires specialized labs. Most community users track CBC + lymphocyte count and subjective infection frequency as practical proxies.

faqs.q: What is the recommended Thymosin Alpha 1 dosage?
faqs.a: Thymosin Alpha 1 dosing varies by experience level. Beginners typically start at 1.6 mg 2x/week, moderate users at 1.6 mg 2x/week, and aggressive protocols use 1.6 mg 3x/week.

faqs.q: How do you reconstitute Thymosin Alpha 1?
faqs.a: Thymosin Alpha 1 typically comes in 5mg or 10mg vials. Add 2mL of bacteriostatic water to the vial. Use the free calculator for exact syringe units based on your desired dose.

summary: Approved in 35 countries, studied in over 11,000 patients across 30+ clinical trials. Thymosin Alpha 1 (Tα1) is a 28-amino-acid peptide your thymus gland produces to prime T-cell and NK cell immunity. The Zadaxin label established 1.6 mg subcutaneously twice weekly as the clinical standard for hepatitis B, with HBeAg seroconversion rates reaching 30 to 40% versus 18% on placebo (PMC4688733).
